steps.body: A thrown ball is the perfect parametric: time t drives BOTH coordinates, but they obey different rules. Horizontally, nothing pushes it — constant velocity: **x = vₓ·t**. Vertically, gravity pulls — constant acceleration: **y = v_y·t − ½g t²**. (We use g ≈ 10 m/s² for clean numbers.)

widget.prompt: A ball has vₓ = 15 m/s. Using x = vₓ·t, where is it horizontally at t = 3 s?

commonErrors.feedback: 18 = 15 + 3 adds. Horizontal position is a PRODUCT: 15·3 = 45 m.
5 = 15/3 divides. Constant velocity means x = 15·3 = 45 m.

steps.body: Why the two motions don't interfere.
explanationVariants: Gravity acts only vertically, so it changes y but never x — the horizontal motion stays uniform regardless of the fall.
Horizontal and vertical are independent: this is why a dropped ball and a ball thrown level hit the ground together.

widget.prompt: Why does the horizontal speed stay constant during flight?

options.label: Gravity acts only vertically, leaving horizontal motion untouched
options.feedback: Right — the sole force is vertical, so x keeps its uniform x = vₓ·t.

options.label: Because air pushes it forward
options.feedback: This imagines a forward force that isn't there — with gravity the only force and it pointing straight down, nothing acts horizontally, so x stays uniform at vₓ·t.

options.label: Because the ball slows down evenly in both directions
options.feedback: Only the VERTICAL motion changes (gravity). Horizontal stays constant.

steps.body: The vertical equation y = v_y·t − ½g t² is a **downward parabola in t** (recall quadratics): it rises, slows, stops at the top, and falls. The vertical velocity is v_y − g t — it hits **zero at the peak**, then goes negative on the way down.

explanationVariants: Plug t = 1: the rise term 20 minus the fall term 5 gives 15 m.

widget.prompt: With v_y = 20 m/s and g = 10, use y = v_y·t − ½g t² to find the height at t = 1 s.

commonErrors.feedback: 20 = v_y·t alone ignores the −½g t² fall term: 20 − 5 = 15 m.
The fall term is ½·10·1² = 5, not 10: 20 − 5 = 15 m.

explanationVariants: At the highest point the vertical velocity is 0 — it's momentarily neither rising nor falling; horizontal velocity is still vₓ.
v_y − g t = 0 defines the peak; the ball still moves sideways at vₓ.

widget.prompt: At the very top of its arc, the ball's VERTICAL velocity is:

options.label: zero
options.feedback: Right — v_y − g t = 0 at the peak; only the horizontal velocity remains.

options.label: maximum
options.feedback: Vertical velocity is zero at the top — it was maximum at LAUNCH and decreased to 0.

options.label: equal to g
options.feedback: g is an acceleration, not the velocity. At the peak the vertical velocity is 0.

explanationVariants: At t = 2 s: x = 15·2 = 30 m and y = 20·2 − 5·2² = 40 − 20 = 20 m. The height is 20 m.
Vertical: 40 rise minus 20 fall = 20 m (this is also the peak, since t = 2 = v_y/g).

widget.prompt: A ball has vₓ = 15, v_y = 20 (g = 10). What is its height y at t = 2 s?

commonErrors.feedback: 30 is the horizontal position x = 15·2. The height is y = 40 − 20 = 20 m.
40 = 20·2 forgets the fall term 5·2² = 20: height is 20 m.

takeaways: Vertical: y = v_y·t − ½g t² (a downward parabola in t).
The two motions are independent; vertical velocity is 0 at the peak.
steps.teaser: Next: extracting the peak height, flight time, and range.

concept.body: Projectile: x = vₓ·t (steady) and y = v_y·t − ½g t² (gravity). Substitute a time into each for the ball's position; vertical velocity v_y − g t is 0 at the top.

widget.prompt: v_y = 10, g = 10. Find y at t = 1 s using y = v_y·t − ½g t².

commonErrors.feedback: 10 = v_y·t alone; subtract the fall term ½·10·1² = 5: height 5 m.
At t = 1 the ball is still up: 10 − 5 = 5 m, not 0.
